There are 2 independent limits here:

* The number of nodes (as calculated in the code snippet above), exceeding this will cause a hard crash that prompted the creation of this PR.
* The depth of the tree (`QuadTree::cStackSize`), exceeding this will cause an assert and possibly missing collisions later. This requires adding at least 3 * `QuadTree::cStackSize` individual bodies through `BodyInterface::AddBody`.

I'm not a big fan of the proposed solution as optimizing the broadphase is an expensive operation and doing it every 256 bodies can incur considerable cost when creating a big world. The most efficient way of adding bodies would be to create an array of `BodyID`s that need to be added and flushing this array using `BodyInterface::AddBodiesPrepare/Finalize` whenever a function is called that actually needs the bodies to be in the world similar to the previous `try_optimize` function (e.g. casting a ray or doing a physics update). This would remove the need to call `PhysicsSystem::OptimizeBroadPhase`.

> The most efficient way of adding bodies would be to create an array of BodyIDs that need to be added and flushing this array using BodyInterface::AddBodiesPrepare/Finalize whenever a function is called that actually needs the bodies to be in the world similar to the previous try_optimize function (e.g. casting a ray or doing a physics update).

That sounds reasonable.

Makes me wonder, how does Jolt normally handle physics bodies being added on the fly though and the need to grow the broad phase tree? How come there is a hard limit on the broadphase size as opposed to just growing it when required as part of Jolt?

_(There may be good reasons for it, I'm just curious - I wrote the BVH used in Godot physics a while back and it uses pools for nodes and leaves.)_

> I'm not a big fan of the proposed solution as optimizing the broadphase is an expensive operation and doing it every 256 bodies can incur considerable cost when creating a big world. The most efficient way of adding bodies would be to create an array of `BodyID`s that need to be added and flushing this array using `BodyInterface::AddBodiesPrepare/Finalize` whenever a function is called that actually needs the bodies to be in the world similar to the previous `try_optimize` function (e.g. casting a ray or doing a physics update). This would remove the need to call `PhysicsSystem::OptimizeBroadPhase`.

For some reason I've always dismissed this option as being too messy, because I wasn't sure how you'd know when to flush the batching, since there's no natural "we're done adding all the bodies now" point with how Godot's physics server integration is done, but yeah, it really is just doing pretty much the same thing as what `JoltSpace3D::try_optimize` is doing already.

I guess the only real gotcha would be the fact that `JPH::BodyInterface::AddBodiesFinalize` either activates all or none of the bodies, so I'm assuming it's best to have two batches, one for the to-be-active bodies and one for the to-be-inactive bodies, ~~otherwise you'd be calling `JPH::BodyInterface::ActivateBody` potentially hundreds of times after adding the batch~~.

That shouldn't take long to throw together.

I've put up a draft of the batching in #107454.

With that, I'll go ahead and close this.

> Makes me wonder, how does Jolt normally handle physics bodies being added on the fly though and the need to grow the broad phase tree? How come there is a hard limit on the broadphase size as opposed to just growing it when required as part of Jolt?

Some of the operations on the broad phase are lock free. Because allocating memory is not lock free, I cannot allocate new nodes on the fly. That's why you specify a max on startup. This allows us to add/remove bodies and do queries from multiple threads at once.
